lesson.title: The Op-Amp That Doesn't Exist: Why Engineers Pretend Anyway
lesson.summary: The ideal op-amp model assumes infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, and zero output impedance; no real device meets these exactly, but real devices come close enough that the idealization makes circuit analysis dramatically simpler without meaningfully sacrificing accuracy.
lesson.body:
No physical operational amplifier has literally infinite gain or draws exactly zero current at its inputs. Yet nearly every hand analysis of an op-amp circuit begins by assuming exactly that. The ideal op-amp model rests on a small set of simplifying assumptions: infinite open-loop gain (A_OL approaches infinity), infinite input impedance (no current flows into either input terminal), zero output impedance (the output behaves like a perfect voltage source regardless of the load it drives), and usually infinite bandwidth as well.

The justification for this idealization is not wishful thinking, it is that real op-amps get close enough that the error introduced is negligible for the overwhelming majority of designs. An open-loop gain of 200,000, while not infinite, is large enough that treating it as infinite changes almost nothing in the final answer, as the closed-loop gain chapter will show numerically. Input bias currents on typical op-amps run from picoamps to a few hundred nanoamps, against source currents in circuits that are often in the milliamp range, a ratio of a million to one or more. Output impedance is commonly under 100 ohms open-loop and drops further once feedback is applied, tiny next to typical load resistances of kilohms.

It helps to see how small the gap really is. Take a real op-amp with A_OL = 200,000 that needs to produce an output of 5 volts. From Vout = A_OL times (V+ minus V-), the required differential input voltage is V+ minus V- = Vout / A_OL = 5 V / 200,000 = 0.000025 V, or 25 microvolts. Compared to the 5 volt output, or to typical signal levels of tenths or whole volts, 25 microvolts is close enough to zero that assuming it is exactly zero introduces an error far smaller than the tolerance of the resistors used to build the rest of the circuit.

The infinite input impedance assumption plays an equally important role, though its effect shows up differently: it means no current is diverted from the source into the op-amp's input pins, so every bit of current supplied by a source flows only through the external resistors we choose to place. This becomes the basis for a current-balance argument used repeatedly in the chapters ahead.

By itself, the ideal op-amp model is only half the story. Infinite open-loop gain describes the bare amplifier, but a bare amplifier with infinite gain would instantly saturate at the slightest input imbalance, exactly the problem raised in the previous chapter. The ideal op-amp only becomes a usable, analyzable building block once it is combined with negative feedback, which is where the next chapter picks up.
